sections.title_en: Preferring the Relative, the Neighbour and the Member of One's People
sections.body_en:
When two people ask a person for a loan and he is able to lend to only one, he should give precedence to the one closer to him. As it is said (Shemot 22:24): "If you lend money to any of My people, to the poor with you." 'With you' means the one close to you. Therefore a relative takes precedence over a neighbour, a neighbour over one who is not a neighbour, one who lives in your city over one who does not live in your city, and a member of your people over a member of another people (Bava Metzia 71a).

Similarly it is said (Vayikra 25:14): "And if you sell something to your fellow, or buy from the hand of your fellow, you shall not wrong one another." The Sages said (in the Sifra) that with the word 'your fellow' the Torah intended to teach that in every purchase or sale a person should prefer his fellow, that is, the one closer to him, and this includes giving precedence to the members of his people over members of another people. The novelty in this is that not only in matters of kindness and tzedaka should one prefer the one close, but in all economic areas too a person should prefer his relatives.

There is in this halakha no expression of boycotting one who is not a relative, or one who is not a neighbour, or a member of another people. On the contrary, it is known that all Israel has responsibility for the repair of the whole world, as it was said to Avraham our father (Bereshit 12:3): "and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed." And likewise it was said to Yaakov our father (ibid. 28:14): "and in you and in your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed." Rather this halakha is intended to express the brotherhood and the extra responsibility that rests on every person towards his relatives, his neighbours and the members of his people. It is reasonable that this is the law also for the members of all the peoples: every person must give precedence, in all matters between a person and his fellow, to his relatives, and afterwards to his neighbours, and afterwards to the members of his people.

The idea of this rule is simple and logical: in order to solve all the distress in the world and build a good and healthy society, one must begin and repair in order, from the near circle to the farther. Beyond the fact that brotherhood requires this, this principle allows society to repair itself completely, as responsibility spreads logically in circles: the closer a person is to his fellow, the more he knows him, and the better he knows how to help him usefully. So it is in matters of tzedaka, and so too in matters of work: in the long term relatives, neighbours and members of the people know how to employ the worker in the way most beneficial to both.

The mitzva to prefer the member of our people applies also when the price he asks is a little more expensive, for we have learned that in lending too it is a mitzva to prefer the Jew (Bava Metzia 71a), and it is known that it is permitted to lend to a gentile with interest whereas to a Jew it is forbidden; if so, when the Torah commands us to give precedence and lend to the member of our people, the intention is even if we lose a certain profit (Ahavat Ḥesed vol. 1, 5:7). However, when the difference between them is not small, there is no obligation to prefer him.

The meaning of this is that the intention is not that the mitzva of preference should disrupt the economic considerations of the person or the business; rather the intention of the mitzva is to create a certain preference for the relative, the neighbour and the member of the people, while preserving the profitability and viability of the business.

Just as it is a mitzva to give precedence to a relative, a neighbour and a member of the people for buying, selling and lending, so and even more it is a mitzva to give them precedence regarding work. For here the mitzva of tzedaka joins in too, since a person who does not find work is close to being considered poor, and consequently it is a mitzva to raise him up and support him.

That is, in preferring a Jewish worker there are two mitzvot: the first, the general mitzva to prefer relatives and members of the people; and the second, tzedaka, which is more obligating. And the finest tzedaka is in giving work. And so the Rambam explained (Gifts to the Poor 10:7) that there are eight levels in tzedaka, each above the other, and the highest level, above which there is none, is to give the poor person work, that is, to find him a permanent source of livelihood, so that he will be able to stand on his own feet by his own strength. And there is in it a further mitzva, as it is said (Vayikra 25:35): "And if your brother becomes poor and his hand fails with you, then you shall uphold him."

Many refrain from employing their relative or a member of their people, because they are uncomfortable to command him to do what they ask of a stranger who is far from them. But the Sages wanted to encourage a person to hire the poor in his surroundings in order to give them a livelihood, as brought in the Mishna (Avot 1:5): "Yose ben Yoḥanan of Jerusalem says: Let your house be wide open, and let the poor be members of your household." And the intention is to prefer to hire them for simple and lowly household work (Bava Metzia 60b). And so the Rambam wrote (Gifts to the Poor 10:17): "The Sages commanded that the members of a person's household be poor people and orphans instead of slaves; it is better for him to make use of these, and let the children of Avraham, Yitzḥak and Yaakov benefit from his property… for whoever increases slaves adds sin and iniquity to the world every single day; and if the poor are members of his household, at every single moment he adds merit and mitzvot."

As regarding buying and selling, this mitzva too applies when the Jewish worker is a little more expensive; but if he is significantly more expensive, or even a little more expensive but this additional cost will harm the economic stability of the business against its competitors, there is no mitzva to give precedence to the relative, the neighbour and the Jew.

About a hundred years ago, in the days of the Second Aliya (5664-5674; 1904-1914), when the Jewish settlement began to become established in the Land, and its development depended to a great extent on finding workplaces for Jews who would be able to immigrate to the Land, various bodies, headed by the workers' movements, began to fight for 'Hebrew labour', both in order to enable the absorption of Jewish workers and in order to prevent the continuation of Arab immigration to the Land of Israel. The struggle intensified when, following the policy set in the 'White Paper', the British government granted immigration certificates to Jews according to the ability to absorb them economically.

But a problem arose: the Arabs agreed to work for much lower wages, and the question was whether it is possible to obligate the farmers and business owners to employ Jewish workers at higher wages. The demand of the Zionist workers' movements was that in every situation and at any price they should employ Jewish workers. To advance their position, they organised demonstrations, sometimes violent, against employers who employed Arab workers. In practice the war against Arab labour failed, and what helped reduce the number of Arab workers were the riots in which Arabs murdered Jews, and also the boycotts that the Arabs themselves imposed on the Jewish settlement. Indeed, the ideological struggle for Hebrew labour strengthened the moral position that prefers employing Jewish workers.

At that time the rabbis too addressed the question, and in the name of our master Rav Kook it was reported that on a certain occasion he said that it is possible to obligate a Jewish employer to pay up to a third more for a Jewish worker. Later his student Rav Yisraeli wrote (Ḥavat Binyamin 1:22) that up to an addition of a sixth it is possible to obligate an employer to hire a Jewish worker.

And according to Rav Ben-Tzion Meir Uziel, who was the Chief Rabbi and Rishon Le-Tziyon at the time of the establishment of the State, it is possible to obligate the employers to hire a Jewish worker at a price at which a Jew can live a reasonable life as is accepted in Jewish society, even if this salary is double the salary of the Arab worker. This is because a mutual responsibility rests on the members of the whole people to take care of one another, and this includes seeing to it that they can live with dignity. That is, the minimum wage, in Rav Uziel's view, need not be influenced by the supply and demand in the market for these workers, or by the competition of the gentile workers; rather the obligation rests on society and the employers to give precedence to a worker from among the members of their people, and to pay him a salary that allows a reasonable standard of living relative to his brothers, the members of his people. As proof of this, Rav Uziel mentioned the halakha regarding the master of a Hebrew slave, who is obligated to provide his slave a standard of living parallel to the master's standard. As the Sages expounded in tractate Kiddushin (Kiddushin 20a): "'For it is good for him with you': with you in food and with you in drink." From this he learned that an employer too must see to it that his worker has a salary from which he can subsist with dignity, relative to what is accepted in the country (Mishpetei Uziel 4:44).

As for the halakha, it seems that it is the obligation of the Jewish state to see to it that all Jews have a dignified livelihood; but this obligation cannot be imposed on the individual employer, who must compete in the market against his competitors who employ much cheaper workers. But the individual too has a mitzva to look for ways to employ his brothers while advancing the business to greater efficiency and profitability.

In the meantime the State of Israel was established, which committed itself to act fairly towards all its residents, including not discriminating against a person because of his sex, religion and race. Nevertheless, the problem of employing Arabs still stands in its place. And although the State as a whole cannot discriminate between its citizens, it is fitting for each and every individual who employs workers to take into account the Torah scale of values, according to which there are three reasons for granting preference to workers who are not Arabs, and all of them stem from the war between Israel and the Arabs over the Land of Israel. First, we are commanded to possess the Land, so that it will be in our hands and not in the hands of another nation, as the Ramban defined the mitzva (above 3:1-2). And since many of the Arabs do not agree that the Land belongs to us, and a struggle over the Land of Israel is still being waged, which at times develops into a bloody war, the mitzva rests on us to prevent as far as possible their hold on the Land, in order to prevent the possibility that they will fight against our dwelling here. And it is clear that by giving places of employment to Arabs who are suspected of hostility towards us, we cause the opposite result: we strengthen their hold on the Land, and do not allow them to think seriously about emigration.

A second mitzva, connected to this, is the mitzva of "lo teḥonnem" (Devarim 7:2), whose meaning is not to give gentiles a foothold in the soil of the Land of Israel. That is, it is forbidden to sell to a gentile who is not a ger toshav land or a house in the Land of Israel, and whoever does not support the State of Israel being the state of the Jews cannot be considered a 'ger toshav' (as explained above 5:1-2). To our sorrow, many of the Arabs living in the Land do not support the State of Israel as the state of the Jews, and do not help it in the struggle for its existence against its enemies as is expected of loyal citizens, and consequently they cannot be considered 'gerim toshavim', and it is forbidden to sell them a house or land in the Land. Giving work too strengthens to some extent their foothold in the Land. For the reality is that following the Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel in the last hundred and fifty years, hundreds of thousands of Arabs immigrated to the Land, who came to seek work in the developing Jewish settlement. One should hope that if the employment of Arabs who do not support the Jewish identity of the State decreases and is replaced as needed by the work of members of other peoples, their emigration to other countries will be accelerated, and those who remain in the Land will be closer to the definition of ger toshav, for whose livelihood it is a mitzva to care. A third reason is the certain concern of attacks that may be carried out by hostile Arab workers or with their help.

All these reasons are said regarding Arabs who are suspected of hostility to the State of Israel; but those who support the State of Israel as the state of the Jewish people are worthy of the status of 'ger toshav', and it is a mitzva to employ them and to do kindness with them.

One should add that although from the outset it is preferable not to employ an Arab who is suspected of hostility and is not worthy of the status of 'ger toshav', in practice, when one employs him, one is obligated to treat him with full respect and fairness. It is forbidden to humiliate him, to oppress him, or to withhold his wages overnight. First, because of the employer's obligation of fairness towards the worker. Second, it may be that he is decent and supports the people of Israel and is worthy of the definition of 'ger toshav', towards whom we are obligated to act not only fairly, but it is even a mitzva to give him tzedaka in time of need (above 5:5, 4).

One should hope that as the years pass, the Arabs who are hostile to us will decrease through repentance or emigration to other countries, and those who love us will remain to live with us in brotherhood.

sections.title_en: Building a House in the Settlements
sections.body_en:
Following the previous halakhot, a question arises from people who want to build their house in Judea and Samaria: must they hire Jewish workers whose price is much higher than the price of Arab workers?1 Some claim that for the reasons mentioned in the previous halakha, one must be careful to hire Jewish workers or members of another people that is not at war with us, even if as a result of this position fewer houses will be built, or a person will be able to buy a smaller house. But in practice, whenever the price of the Jewish workers is significantly higher, it is preferable to build the house in the settlement with local Arab workers, because in the end our central aim is to strengthen the Jewish hold on the Land. Indeed, in all the trades in which Jewish workers are not significantly more expensive, one should try to prefer them. And likewise it is fitting to take trouble over developing modern and industrialised building methods that will require fewer workers.

Refraining from employing Arab workers will also not help, since the position of the heads of the security establishment is that it is desirable to give work to a certain total of Arab workers from Judea and Samaria; and if Jews in Judea and Samaria employ a thousand fewer of them, then instead of granting, for example, fifty thousand work permits to workers from China, the State of Israel will grant only forty-nine thousand work permits, in order to be able to grant another thousand work permits to Arabs from Judea and Samaria. Thus this policy is in the hands of the State, and the influence of the individual on the national situation in this area is very small. And who knows, perhaps after the fact, giving work to Arab workers will indeed help reduce violence and bring hearts closer (above 5:5, 4).

May it be His will that we merit, and the words of the prophet Yeshayahu be fulfilled in us (65:21-25): "And they shall build houses and inhabit them, and they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for as the days of a tree shall be the days of My people, and My chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands… The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all My holy mountain, says the Lord." And the members of the peoples who are hostile to us will return in repentance and come to help build our Land, as it is said (ibid. 60:10): "And foreigners shall build your walls, and their kings shall minister to you." And it is said (ibid. 61:5): "And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners shall be your ploughmen and your vinedressers."

notes_en.en: There are several reasons for the high price of Jewish workers compared with Arab workers who live in Judea and Samaria. First, Jews are accustomed to living at a higher standard of living and consequently demand higher wages. Second, most of the Jewish workers live in the big cities, and in order to bring them to the building sites in Judea and Samaria, one must organise transport that costs a great deal of money, and one must also pay them for the travel time. By contrast, the Arab workers live close to the building area, so that in addition to their receiving a lower salary, their employment also saves the transport. Third, the Jewish workers are liable to all the taxes, whereas the Arabs are not liable to them. All these considerations together create a significant difference.
